title: In/tension modeling: what gives us the right?
text:
In/tension modeling: what gives us the right?

How to navigate opposing voices and lived tensions.

By Julia Beard, Naman Mandhan, & Stacie Sheldon

Asking the Hardest Question First

“What gives us the right to make the interventions and choices we are contemplating on behalf of others?” asks Erika Hall, cofounder of Mule Design. For UX professionals, it’s a question worth sitting with. We’re driven by empathy and a desire to solve problems, yet it’s not common practice for us to question our own authority. How often do we stop to ask the question Erika poses — especially when so much of our job involves putting solutions out into the world? In our effort to do good, we risk unintentionally causing harm. Do we recognize how much power and privilege come with that responsibility?

In Part One of In/Tension Modeling as a UX research and strategy tool, we explored the reality that when you solve one problem, other problems are naturally created. We also discussed how, while analyzing data, you will often find perspectives that are in conflict with one another, and how it is vital to amplify all perspectives, not just the loud ones.

In this Part Two, we go a step deeper into how In/Tension Modeling can be applied to anticipate, prevent, and respond to potential harms while creating solutions. Throughout the design process, it offers a way to continually check the work against Erika’s question: “What gives us the right?” — ensuring that the drive to solve problems is balanced with care for those most affected by the outcomes.

Throughout this article, we share examples of how In/Tension Modeling helped us navigate conflicting perspectives and advocate for the lived experiences of those most affected by the outcomes of a solution. While reading these examples you’ll find moments where we often questioned our own authority on highly polarizing topics. Instead of taking sides, we sought to make space for all the voices and used practical tools to find paths forward that minimize harm. These stories demonstrate that staying with the tension, rather than rushing to resolve it, can lead to more inclusive and resilient outcomes.

How In/Tension Modeling Works: A Quick Map

The stories in this article move through three recurring steps. You’ll see each of them in action as you read.

Step 1: Surface moments of tension

While interacting with research findings, we may encounter opinions or experiences that contradict one another. A common question that arises is how to navigate these conflicting needs and goals, which can feel paralyzing. One effective approach is to juxtapose these perspectives. Doing so allows us to see the full spectrum of needs and goals, leading to better understanding and more informed decision-making. Learn more about this step in Part One of In/Tension Modeling as a UX Research and Strategy Tool.

Step 2: Identify opportunities and cultivate solutions

Where there is tension, there is opportunity. Moments of conflict often reveal pain points, but by reframing those pain points as opportunities, we shift from what is not working to what could work better. This mindset helps us approach problem solving with curiosity instead of frustration, and it keeps conversations constructive.

Once opportunities have been identified, brainstorm ways to address them. Each opportunity becomes a prompt for generating solution ideas that balance the needs and values represented in the voices from research.

Step 3: Assess solution feasibility

Once solutions have been brainstormed, take time to consider how each one might affect all parties involved. A helpful way to do this is by exploring the relationships between conflicting points of view and using the Range of Tolerance tool to see where each voice falls. This helps identify whether a proposed solution might unintentionally exclude or disadvantage someone.

Involving a diverse group at this stage can surface different perspectives and reduce bias. It is also important to remember that solving one problem can sometimes create another. Revisit the preferences and tolerance ranges of each voice to ensure the solution remains balanced and practical.

Repeat step three for all solutions.

Central to Step 3 is a tool designed to make that assessment visible across every voice in the room: the Range of Tolerance.

The Range of Tolerance

The strength of the Range of Tolerance lies in its honesty. Full agreement is rare. Rather than seeking solutions everyone loves, it helps identify solutions that people can genuinely accept while intentionally mitigating harm or exclusion. When a voice falls outside the range of tolerance, it signals that a proposed solution may lead to disengagement, resistance, or loss of participation.

When testing the viability of solutions, the project team looked for options where all voices fall within either the preference zone or the range of tolerance.

  • Preference zone: The proposed solution is ideal for that group.
  • Range of tolerance zone: While the proposed solution may not be their preferred option, they can live with it and it is unlikely to cause harm.
  • Outside both zones: Anything outside the range of tolerance means they are not willing to consent to that solution.

It is difficult to find solutions that place every voice in the preference zone, especially when perspectives are in conflict. But aiming for solutions that keep all voices within the range of tolerance is a practical and powerful goal. It allows us to design with all perspectives in mind, rather than feeling forced to choose one over another; or worse, abandoning the effort to design a solution at all.

Responsible design does not pick sides and does not ignore harms. It works through the tension.

When Every Voice Tells a Different Story: A Case from the Field

Tension isn’t always a bad thing; it can actually bring important truths to the surface. The role of a researcher is not to be a peacekeeper–it is to sit with conflicting insights and find a way forward through them. One project brought this challenge into sharp focus: we were asked to work on one of the most polarizing government programs out there, child support. By design, the program can feel like it creates a winner and a loser. If you are paying support, you may feel you are paying too much or that the money is not being spent as intended. If you are receiving support, you may feel you are not getting nearly enough to meet your family’s needs. Those opposing experiences, both valid, make the program emotionally charged for everyone involved.

Even people who have never participated in the Child Support Program often carry assumptions shaped by what they have heard from friends, family, or the media. Phrases such as “deadbeat parent” or “they get so much in child support, they probably don’t even spend it on the kids” seep into everyday conversations and influence how we see the system, often in ways that are oversimplified or unfair.

Choosing not to act would still leave children bearing the consequences.

For this qualitative research project, our goal was to help child support employees build empathy with families by sharing the stories of people who had lived experience with the program. We also recognized that while navigating child support could be incredibly difficult for participants, the work could be emotionally complex and demanding for staff. Heavy workloads and highly sensitive situations could influence how families experienced the system. We were asked to create a storytelling exhibit to help reconnect staff with the human side of their work. To tell these stories authentically, we first needed to listen.

The foundation of this research was one-on-one interviews with families connected to the program. We spoke with people who pay child support, who receive it, and who do both. We sought a diversity of voices which included moms, dads, family members with guardianship, individuals who had left the program, and participants whose involvement ranged from just one year to over thirty.

As we conducted interviews, we repeatedly heard perspectives that were in direct tension with one another. In one conversation, a parent who pays child support shared that their monthly payments were so high they were being pushed into debt and struggling to maintain a stable home. In the very next interview, a parent who receives child support described that same payment structure as leaving them without enough money to cover basic needs like food, rent, and childcare. Each parent’s experience was real and valid, shaped by their own circumstances, and each revealed how the system could place families in competing positions. Somewhere in the middle of that tension was a child, depending on both.

As a researcher when someone shares a deeply personal experience, especially one that impacts their entire family, you feel a responsibility to honor that. It is not just about listening; it is about carrying their voice forward in a meaningful way. In this case, that responsibility felt heavy. Every possible solution carried a risk. Solving for one group could unintentionally hurt another. And that harm was real. It could mean one group going into overwhelming debt or the other group not having the support needed to care for their family. Choosing not to act would still leave children bearing the consequences.

This led us to consider a framework authored by Designit entitled Do No Harm. The framework challenges practitioners to think about the consequences not only of their actions, but also of their inaction. It encourages us to keep moving forward, even if we make mistakes, as long as we do not become passive.

“If the design discipline is to evolve into a safer and more conscientious version of itself, we need to develop approaches from within to be able to effectively forecast, prevent, and respond to harm. A disciplinary culture shift is in order, and the Do No Harm framework provides a way towards achieving it.” — Dr. Pardis Shafafi​, Global Responsible Business Lead of Designit

After careful reflection, we recognized that doing nothing (not directly addressing the tensions) carried greater consequences than taking action . We chose to adopt the Do No Harm framework with In/Tension Modeling and committed to amplifying the lived experiences we uncovered. That choice gave us a clear path forward; not the easy path, not the fast path, but the honest, difficult, and necessary one. Through In/Tension Modeling, we didn’t just identify points of tension; we stayed with them, worked through them, and sought to fully understand every perspective.

The result was a storytelling exhibit built for program staff, organized around the voices of payers, receivers, and people who had experienced both. It wasn’t designed to declare a winner. It was designed to make the full range of lived experiences impossible to ignore, inviting staff to sit with the people behind the cases rather than the cases alone. The exhibit included reflection questions, guiding principles for engagement, and a call to action for teams ready to do something with what they heard. We built it to last beyond the project. The voices we had been trusted to carry forward were at its heart.

That process, staying with the tension long enough to honor every voice, is what In/Tension Modeling made possible. And it wasn’t the last time we’d need it.

When Empathy Is Not Enough

Even with a strong foundation in empathy and a commitment to honoring every voice, there are moments when progress stalls. Tensions can become so entrenched — politically, emotionally, or institutionally, that traditional methods of facilitation and consensus-building fall short.

In another project with a statewide Child Support Program, we encountered exactly this kind of deeply entrenched disagreement over whether families receiving state assistance should be required to participate in the Program. Despite clear direction and shared intentions, the people involved struggled to move forward. The deeper we went, the more it became evident that no amount of storytelling or surface-level agreement could bridge the divide. We applied In/Tension Modeling not only as a research tool, but as a strategic intervention to help people see one another’s perspectives more clearly, and to begin moving past their entrenched positions.

The disagreement surfaced when we were helping to shape a future vision for how services would be delivered. In the first phase, we conducted research to understand how staff across the program perceived the current system, while also gathering experiences from the families being served. This work revealed a deeply divided landscape. Two dominant narratives had taken hold, and neither side seemed willing or able to move toward common ground.

On one side, some of these stakeholders expressed a desire to change the experience for families receiving state assistance. They described how participation in the program is mandatory for those on assistance, since the state seeks reimbursement through child support collections. Many believe that families often do not understand this requirement when they apply for assistance, or that they lack a real choice because the financial support is essential. Some participants questioned whether this approach truly benefits families, arguing that it can cause harm by reducing autonomy and dignity without generating significant financial return for the state.

At the same time, other stakeholders expressed a different perspective: the program should not change because individuals who use and benefit from the services of the state have an obligation to help repay those costs. For this perspective, required participation was not viewed as punitive but as necessary for fairness, accountability, and in some cases protection. They noted that mandatory engagement with state systems can, in certain situations such as cases of family violence, create opportunities for safety, support, or intervention that might not otherwise occur.

We wondered how to get past this argument. The more it was discussed the more entrenched it felt. We decided a starting point should be to model the two sides of the debate:

As a third party this was our best effort to represent the two sides and we were as intentional as possible to write each voice without bias, knowing that we could not write each side exactly how a person might want to see it represented.

One learning we took from this experience was that, next time, we might invite working groups to participate in creating the models themselves. In our case, we did not have enough time to do so (and it remains to be seen if it would have been beneficial or created a sticking point) but the models as written did produce an immediate response. One person said, “I don’t see my idea on here. There is a loophole where we can avoid forcing them into this program if we wish.” We had never heard that idea before and it became a voice in the middle as well as the beginning of a possible solution for today while the deeper issue is still debated.

Facing Our Own Biases in the Process

While modeling opposing voices in the child support project helped move the conversation forward, it also revealed something we hadn’t anticipated, our own blind spots. As researchers and facilitators, we’re trained to center empathy and maintain neutrality, but the charged nature of this work pushed us into uncomfortable territory.

When tensions mirrored our own deeply held beliefs, it became painfully clear how hard it is to give fair representation to perspectives we personally disagree with. This wasn’t just about the issues at hand, it was a mirror for our own assumptions, and a test of our integrity in the process.

We found that when working as organizational and strategic researchers on issues like child support, the emotions run deep, both within the Child Support Program itself and within us as humans doing the work. Perspectives on poverty, personal autonomy, individual agency, and the role of government collided in ways that brought many tensions to the surface, and we often felt those tensions as sharply as the people we were listening to.

At one point, facing a major impasse, we turned to modeling the most common positions emerging from our sessions. Writing one side came naturally — it reflected our own views. But the opposing voice? We struggled. Early drafts framed it as misguided, even harmful. That moment revealed just how easily bias can seep in, even with the best intentions.

And yet, that struggle was the work.

And yet, that struggle was the work. Wrestling with perspectives we disagreed with forced us to slow down, to listen more carefully, and to understand not just what people believed, but why. It demanded more than empathy — it demanded rigor. We’ve come to believe that this kind of effort should be part of the process itself. Having working groups model both their own and opposing voices, then reflect on that experience, could be transformative. For us, it deepened our respect for every position at the table and gave us a better foundation for moving forward together.

Lessons Learned
#1 Even when every effort is made to listen and honor each voice, some conflicts are rooted so deeply in belief systems, institutional structures, or moral divides that empathy alone cannot bridge them.
#2 Creating neutral models of each perspective helped shift the group from argument to reflection. It gave participants a way to see their own positions more clearly and to recognize the logic in others’ views.
#3 Writing from perspectives that differed from our own revealed our blind spots. The exercise forced us to confront how easily personal beliefs can shape research outputs, even unconsciously.
#4 The discomfort of disagreement and resistance is not a barrier to progress but a source of information about what truly matters to people. Learning to stay with that discomfort, rather than smoothing it over, can produce deeper understanding and more resilient solutions.

Two Truths: Power & Privilege.

Two things are true but rarely discussed in UX: our roles carry both power and privilege. That power is not always visible, but it is embedded in our roles and the decisions we make every day. Designing for others means making choices that can either support or constrain their lives. That responsibility requires care, humility, and an awareness of our influence because everything we create has the potential to shape someone’s life for better or worse.

“All powers have two sides, the power to create and the power to destroy. We must recognize them both, but invest our gifts on the side of creation.” — Robin Wall Kimmerer, Braiding Sweetgrass

Robin Wall Kimmerer is a botanist and member of the Citizen Potawatomi Nation whose writing explores reciprocity between humans and the natural world. Her words travel well beyond their original context, and that, too, is worth noticing.

On a project with an automotive company, we conducted qualitative research to understand drivers’ behaviors, needs, and perceptions of electric vehicles. We spoke with EV, hybrid, and gas-powered drivers and uncovered a wide range of deeply held, often conflicting attitudes: some saw driving an EV as something they could personally do to contribute to a better environmental future, while others depended on gas-powered vehicles to do their jobs and support their families.

To capture these tensions, we plotted perspectives on an “In/Tension” scale. Three distinct voices emerged:

It was tempting to connect most with the first voice because it aligned with our own values and lived experiences. But designing only for those who think like us risks reinforcing privilege and overlooking important voices. In/Tension modeling reminds us to ask whether we are designing for people who live like us or for the full range of experiences. It also helps track and map how much each voice can tolerate a given solution, which not only supports more inclusive and sustainable design decisions but also reduces the risk of people abandoning a product or reverting to unhelpful behaviors when a solution pushes beyond what they can accept.

The car example, and the earlier example around child support, show why it is often not the behavior itself that should be judged or dismissed. Our job is to dig deeper to understand why people act the way they do. Why is someone behind on child support payments? Why is someone opposed to EVs? Jumping straight into solutions without that understanding can lead to harm.

A person’s behavior is often shaped by three things: what they are able to do, the circumstances that give them or limit their chances to do it, and the personal drive they feel to act. These elements of capability, opportunity, and motivation work together to influence behaviors. Assuming any of them can cause us to miss the real issue or design a solution that makes things worse. Yet when we understand them, we can remove barriers and, in some cases, help shift an unhelpful behavior into a constructive one.

Following each voice in the EV research revealed these deeper factors. For many EV drivers, the switch aligned with personal values and came with few sacrifices. They drove infrequently, had access to free chargers, and found the change easy. For some gas-powered drivers, however, driving was their livelihood. Charging times meant lost income, and towing for work drained battery life. For them, an EV would threaten their ability to provide for their families.

Understanding these motivations brought empathy into the process. It showed that even when lived experiences differ, the values behind them — responsibility, care for others, doing what is right — can be deeply aligned. It also challenged us to ask a harder question: Are we truly bettering society if our solutions only work for those who already share our worldview? If our work deepens divides rather than bridging them, we may be reinforcing the very systems we hope to improve.

Lessons Learned
#1 Solutions that reflect only our own values and lived experiences risk reinforcing privilege and deepening divides.
#2 Whether someone is behind on child support payments or rejects EVs, the behavior alone is not enough to understand the problem. Deep research into people’s circumstances and constraints offers a clearer view of the “why,” fostering empathy and reducing the risk of harmful assumptions.
#3 Capability, opportunity, and motivation drive behavior. These three factors work together to influence choices. Assuming them can lead to harmful or ineffective solutions, while understanding them can help remove barriers and encourage constructive change.
#4 Mapping how much different perspectives can tolerate a solution allows for more inclusive and sustainable design.
#5 Design should connect people across differences rather than reinforcing existing inequalities. The goal is to bridge, not widen, divides.

When It’s Easier to Choose, and Better Not To

While we as UX professionals play a critical role in confronting power, privilege, and opposing viewpoints in our work, it’s equally important to recognize that we operate within a broader ecosystem — one shaped by human relationships, business objectives, technologies, and cultural norms. For us to effectively practice In/Tension Modeling and ask “What gives us the right?” before “How might we?” we need a culture that supports and protects our ability to create that space.

A recent project offers a compelling example, while translating research insights into new product features for a customer onboarding experience on an e-procurement platform. During synthesis, it was discovered that customers had diverging preferences for how they wanted to add users to their accounts. Some customers knew exactly who they wanted to add and preferred assigning roles and permissions to specific individuals (a user-first approach). Others had a clear idea of the roles and permissions needed but not who would fill them (a role-first approach).

This insight revealed an opportunity to innovate — to meet the needs of those who wanted to assign roles to specific users immediately, and those who needed the flexibility to define roles that could be assigned later. In other words, it was a chance to design for the middle space where tensions and nuance lived.

However, when the author presented these findings to the team, they were asked to “pick a side and recommend it.” Rather than exploring a solution that embraced the tension and expanded the range of tolerance, internal biases and power dynamics took over. The process of translating research into product features shifted — from solving real customer problems across the In/Tension spectrum to prioritizing features that satisfied the preferences of the most powerful stakeholders.

This example shows how cultural forces within teams such as a bias toward quick decisions, deference to power, or discomfort with ambiguity, can collapse the very tension that leads to better, more inclusive outcomes. Practicing In/Tension Modeling isn’t just about having the right methods; it’s about fostering a culture that makes space for complexity, dialogue, and dissent. That kind of culture won’t always be in place, but naming what’s missing is a step toward building it. Even when we can’t fully hold the tension, choosing to surface it is still meaningful. A hope would be that every conversation that resists oversimplification helps shift the culture, bit by bit, toward one that can hold more.

A Practice, Not a Position

So, what gives us the right?

Erika Hall’s question doesn’t have a clean answer, and we’ve stopped expecting one. What we’ve found instead is that the question itself is the practice. Every time we return to it, before a solution, after a finding, in the middle of a disagreement, it keeps us accountable to the people whose lives our work touches. The right, when it exists at all, isn’t ours to keep. We hold it on their behalf, and the work is to be worthy of that.

The work is rarely as simple as deciding who is right and who is wrong. Holding tension does not mean finding the perfect middle ground or choosing which side wins. It means staying curious long enough to understand what different perspectives reveal, particularly when they challenge our own assumptions.

Across every project in this article, child support families navigating an impossible system, drivers weighing livelihood against climate, customers whose needs got flattened into a stakeholder preference, what we found was the same: the most important insights lived exactly where the tension was hardest to hold. Not on either side of it. In it.

We don’t think that changes. We think that’s the work. And we think the practitioners who are willing to stay there, rather than reach for the cleaner answer, are the ones who will build something worth building.

What gives you the right? That question belongs to you now.

text:
Verity Stars Anne Hathaway, Dakota Johnson, & Josh Hartnett Lean Into Its Absurdity

Verity, based on Colleen Hoover’s novel, is currently getting mixed reviews. Some hail it as a “campy, faithful adaptation,” and others are writing it off as “a criminal waste” of stars Dakota Johnson, Josh Hartnett, and Anne Hathaway. The movie follows renowned author Verity Crawford (Anne Hathaway) and Lowen Ashleigh (Dakota Johnson), a struggling writer who relocates to a remote estate to ghostwrite for Verity, putting her in close proximity to the author’s mysterious husband, Jeremy (Hartnett). A sexy thriller starring three of the biggest stars in the world that doesn’t take itself too seriously? Sign us up. Despite the discourse, there’s something undeniably fun about watching three wildly charismatic actors throw themselves into a deliciously messy thriller — and, thankfully, the cast seems to be having just as much fun with it as we did.

When R29 senior fashion writer, Victoria Montalti, sat down with Johnson, Hathaway, and Hartnett, it quickly became clear that the off-screen chemistry is every bit as entertaining as the on-screen tension. The trio traded jokes, teased each other, and proved that even when you’re talking about obsession, secrets, and murder, there’s always room for a little chaos. Johnson, Hathaway, and Hartnett bring an easy, playful energy to the conversation that makes it hard not to imagine what it was like on set, and their press tour has already delivered plenty of chaotic, meme-worthy moments, proving this trio is more than willing to lean into the absurdity.

From zodiac signs to their characters’ questionable choices, the three stars were more than willing to play along. Consider this your invitation to leave the discourse at the door, embrace the camp, and hear what the cast of Verity really thinks about the movie, their characters, and each other.

Refinery29:  There are so many twists and turns in this movie. Is there a moment that you remember in theaters seeing a movie and just like being blown away by a plot twist?

Anne Hathaway: The Others. The Nicole Kidman film from the early 2000s. I remember I went to a showing in the middle of the day. A very well-known actor came in and sat down next to me, and I was like 17, so obviously I knew who he was and not the other way around. 

Josh Hartnett: Was it me? You keep pointing at me. 

AH: You’re just the man to my right the way he was. But yes, Josh, this is how we met. I can’t believe it worked [laughs]. Anyway, there’s this real jump scare that happens where a character comes out of a cupboard — I don’t want to say any more than that —  and this very famous actor and I both screamed and grabbed each other and held each other. And then made eye contact and we’re like, “That happened.” [laughs]

Dakota Johnson: A plot twist, I don’t remember, but I do remember my older brother [went] on a date to the movies with a girl, and he had to bring me. And he put me in a movie theater to watch some cartoon, and then they went into a movie theater and watched Very Bad Things. And then I went into the movie theater. I was eight. 

AH: Oh my God. 

JH: Oh my God. 

DJ: I know. And that ruined my life. Trauma. It ruined my life. 

And then you became a movie star. 

JH: Mine’s the same as Annie’s essentially because it’s The Sixth Sense. It’s basically the same twist. Dead people. 

DJ: I loved that movie! 

Our readers are obsessed with astrology. In the movie, Lowen breezes over the fact that it was her birthday. She does not care. She doesn’t want to celebrate. But do you think she would be into astrology? And what do you think her sign is? 

DJ: I’m gonna say she’s a Sagittarius. Or maybe she’s a Pisces. 

I was thinking Capricorn or Aquarius ’cause they’re both a little weird. Aquariuses don’t like filling in silences. I’m an Aquarius.

DJ: She’s probably an Aquarius, and she probably doesn’t give a fuck.

AH: I think Lowen secretly cares about her birthday. 

DJ: Yeah, everyone does [laughs]. 

Josh, a lot of your characters in movies are the nice guy on the surface, and then underneath, hiding some deep, dark secrets. What draws you to characters like Jeremy? 

JH: It’s more fun to play characters that have depth and complexity, but I don’t know. How old are you? Can I ask?

I’m 27 [laughs]. 

JH: It’s been a trajectory to get to a point where they’ve allowed me to play much more complex characters. At the beginning of my career, I wasn’t allowed any of that. I was always playing the hero, you know? And I think it’s so much fun to be able to play characters that the more you get into them, the deeper and darker they get. 

DJ: You didn’t feel like Trip Fontaine [from The Virgin Suicides] was dark?

JH: Oh, Trip Fontaine had some darkness, for sure. But that was like a kid with a mistake. He regrets it for the rest of his life. That’s the whole backstory. That’s why Trip, as an old man, is talking about it.

AH: I was also gonna say, I also think that because you’ve put in your hero time, it makes the villain time so much richer because we look at you in a certain way, and we’re like, “Oh, Josh is here to save the day.” And then we’re like, “Oh no, he’s gonna kill us all.” 

Anne, you’re pregnant. You’re a mother. Was it difficult playing kind of like the opposite kind of character as a mother? Verity is kind of all over the place and I’m sure very different from how you approach parenthood. 

AH: Verity’s very aware of the darkness of what’s inside of the manuscript. I’m very grateful that I don’t relate to that darkness. I’ve learned, after doing this for so many years, how to keep the characters internal without having it come anywhere near my real life. Especially because some of these things, they feel so horrible that you’re just very happy for it to be over, and then you just wipe the slate and never look back.

title: Verity’s Anne Hathaway And Dakota Johnson Know Seeking Validation Can Be Your Downfall
text:
Verity’s Anne Hathaway And Dakota Johnson Know Seeking Validation Can Be Your Downfall

Major spoilers ahead. Anticipated book-to-screen adaptation Verity hits theaters this week, and stars Anne Hathaway and Dakota Johnson aren’t shy about unpacking the themes in Colleen Hoover’s story. It follows Verity Crawford (Hathaway), a successful novelist who becomes paralysed and unable to finish her book series. Her husband, Jeremy Crawford (Josh Hartnett), hires Lowen Ashleigh (Johnson) to move into their remote property and finish the last book.

When Lowen discovers a manuscript seemingly written by Verity about her life and extremely dark thoughts, she’s left wondering who really lives in the house. The big twist involves a letter that Lowen finds at the end, leaving her wondering whether the manuscript was truly Verity’s story or if it was a writing exercise. Who is the actual villain in the story: Jeremy or Verity? If we believe Jeremy, we follow a narrative that Verity needed validation and constantly sought approval from external forces.

When Lowen reads the manuscript, she feels that Verity is desperate for Jeremy’s love. “The way she’s written herself is wanting Jeremy’s approval,” Johnson tells Refinery29. “She worships him.”

Co-star Hathaway doesn’t think this type of behaviour is healthy. “I think chasing most things is probably not great. Especially something like validation, because I think that you should optimally be around people [where] you don’t have to chase it,” the actor says. “You have to know how to validate yourself.”

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Refinery29 Australia (@refinery29au)

Johnson chimes in with an answer that sounds almost therapised. “I think chasing validation is trying to fill a void that will never be filled by validation,” she declares. “Outwardly looking for validation is never gonna give you what you’re looking for, is what I’ve learned.”

Fans have consistently debated over whether they’re Team Letter or Team Manuscript, and Hathaway openly declares she’s Team Letter, believing that Verity is the victim. “[Wanting Jeremy’s approval] was actually the part that makes me Team Letter. And that whole thing about playing games with him, that to me was like a big red flag,” Hathaway says.

The actor thinks we need to learn to be content without relying on others’ opinions. While you might not be happy with the results of what you’re doing, and may not receive all the accolades you wanted, it’s key to be proud that you tried and did your best.

“I will see value in that. It’s not necessarily about having the best outcome; it’s more about [if] you were proud of the person you were along the way,” she explains.

Verity is in theaters October 2nd.

title: Venus Retrograde In Scorpio & Libra Will Cause The Most Erratic Time Of Year
text:
Venus Retrograde In Scorpio & Libra Will Cause The Most Erratic Time Of Year

The long-awaited Venus retrograde is here, making it the most frenetic and erratic time of 2026. Venus backstrokes in Scorpio and Libra from October 3rd to November 13th, making our lives unpredictable and stressful. Uncuffing season has begun while exes lurk our social media. Welcome to the deep end of the ocean.

The three weeks when Venus retrograde will moonwalk in Scorpio bring power struggles. Venus squares Mars in Leo on October 10th, the day of the New Moon in Libra and the 10/10 portal of endings, highlighting the insatiable passion that lies beneath the surface and in our hearts. The caveat is that we may take our emotions to the extreme, arguing our feelings to get our way or letting go of a partnership because it’s not in alignment with our plans. 

Venus and Pluto in Aquarius link up for the second of the three fraught aspects they share (the first was September 15th, and the third will be December 9th — look to September 15th to unlock the mystery of what is coming, as similar themes may arise). The combination of Venus and Pluto brings out our subconscious fears, resentments, and yearnings. Pluto thrives in triangular situations, so watch out for tea on cheating, secrets, and gossip to come out. 

The best day of the backslide is October 23rd, when the sun and Venus come together, forming an aspect called “cazimi,” which translates from Latin to English as “in the heart of the sun.” This planetary association creates a Venus star point, a term coined by astrologer and author Arielle Guttman. We’re looking at an eight-year cycle in which Venus makes five conjunctions to the sun, forming a pentagram across the zodiac wheel. Here’s how it works: we look back every four years to pick up stories and plots that persist, so pay attention to what happened in 2022 and 2018, as well as every four to eight years before that. 

Interestingly, Venus in Scorpio retrograde squared Mars in Aquarius on October 10th, 2018, and formed a Venus Star Point (”cazimi”) in Scorpio on October 26th, 2018. Expansive Jupiter was at the tail end of its journey in Scorpio. In 2022, the Venus Star Point in Scorpio transpired on October 23rd in certain parts of the world, days before the solar eclipse in Scorpio. 

The claws of justice (which is the theme of Scorpio) will be alive once again, giving us the strength to reassess the role of controversial political and public figures that are behaving unsavory. Venus is the planet of social graces, and it’s opening our eyes by making us as a society aware of who doesn’t fit the bill. Basically, scandals are coming out, exposing those who’ve acted very badly or done humiliating activities. 

Venus backs up into Libra on October 25th, reaffirming and rebalancing relationships until November 13th. This is the messier part of the odyssey because we have the evidence and information from Venus in Scorpio; now we must decide what to do with it and whether we can move forward. Also, Mercury retrograde in Scorpio stretches from October 24th to November 13th, adding more confusion and uncertainty to the mayhem. 

There is an opportunity to heal on October 28th, from Venus retrograde’s opposition to the centaur Chiron, which is in retrograde in Aries. However, we might uncover past traumas that cause more harm than good because they trigger wounds. October 28th is a temporary band-aid to prevent further damage. Still, the apologies and compassion will be short-lived — especially since October 26th’s Full Moon in Taurus reminds us of former and current heartbreaks. Exes will be ever-present, asking for one more chance or closure. Tread lightly and with caution. 

The post-retrograde zone finishes on December 15th in Libra. The pre-shadow began on August 31st. As you can see, this is a long process of emotional building and development. Be kind to yourself by implementing self-care as a radical form of love. Protect your peace by being selective in who you give time to.

title: Your October Horoscope Is Here — & It May Feel Like A Roller Coaster
text:
Your October Horoscope Is Here — & It May Feel Like A Roller Coaster

There are certain months that call for bold action, and others that force us to reflect, release, and get brutally honest about what’s no longer working. October is the latter, but it is not passive. Libra Season carries us through the first three weeks of the month, keeping beauty, harmony, relationships, and balance at the forefront. The equinox energy is still helping us adjust to a new season of life, and Libra reminds us that flexibility can be a form of wisdom. At the same time, October feels like a Scorpio Season prequel because Mercury and Venus are already in Scorpio as the month begins, and Venus stations retrograde there on October 3rd.

Venus retrograde is one of the biggest relationship tests in astrology, but it can also expose which connections are strong enough to deepen. Friendships, finances, creative projects, attraction, intimacy, and unresolved feelings can all come under review, especially with Scorpio adding more emotional intensity to the process. People from the past may circle back, old resentments may resurface, or you may realize you need firmer boundaries with someone. Try not to burn every bridge just because you’re caught up in the feeling of the moment. Let yourself feel what comes up, though. Scorpio energy wants the truth, and sometimes that means admitting what still hurts, what you still desire, what you’re ready to forgive, and what genuinely needs to stay in the past.

The Libra New Moon on October 10th, a potent 10/10 portal date, brings a much-needed reset around peace, relationships, and decision-making. Even though this New Moon is ruled by Venus retrograde in Scorpio, it can help some of us release grudges, recommit to a path we have been circling for a while, or create more harmony by considering how other people may be feeling instead of viewing everything solely through our own emotional lens.

Mid-month, Pluto ends its five-month retrograde in Aquarius, a quieter but important collective shift that can make the transformations we’ve been doing internally feel more achievable in the real world. And through all of this, Mars remains in Leo all month long, giving us one steady source of courage. We don’t have to become victims of every delay, redirection, or emotional plot twist; there’s still plenty we can actively do to move toward the life we want.

By October 23rd, Scorpio Season officially begins, and Mercury begins its retrograde in Scorpio the very next day. The final stretch of the month is more about unfinished business than racing ahead, so expect conversations, plans, financial matters, or emotional storylines to require another look. Then the Taurus Full Moon on October 26th brings us back down to earth after weeks of intensity. It can help us stabilize, simplify, and remember what is actually solid beneath all the emotional noise. October may feel like a roller coaster, but by the end of it, you’ll have a clearer sense of what’s worth fighting for, what’s worth repairing, and what you’re finally ready to stop carrying.

Read your horoscopes for your Sun and Rising signs for the most in-depth forecast.

DashDividers_1_500x100

Aries Sun & Rising:

Aries, October may reveal that some of the battles exhausting you were never meant to be fought this hard in the first place. Venus retrogrades in Scorpio at the beginning of the month, and Mercury follows with its own Scorpio retrograde near month’s end, creating an ongoing review around intimacy, vulnerability, shared energy, and the ways your emotional life affects your overall well-being. You may notice where you’ve been pushing through exhaustion, denying yourself pleasure, carrying someone else’s problems, or being much harsher with yourself internally than anyone realizes. These retrogrades are here to expose the roots of those patterns so you can relate to yourself — and others — from a healthier place.

Mid-month, Pluto stations direct in Aquarius in your friendship, community, and future-oriented realm. After months of privately questioning where you belong and what kind of audience or community you actually want around you, you may feel more willing to show up boldly again. That could mean posting more freely, voicing an opinion that does not fit neatly into the crowd, or pursuing a vision even if nobody else fully understands it yet. You’ve already done some of the underworld work around belonging; now you get to pave your own lane.

Once Scorpio Season begins on October 23rd, you may crave more privacy, emotional depth, and honesty around sexuality, trust, or work you have been procrastinating on because it requires your full attention. Then the Taurus Full Moon on October 26th illuminates your money and security sector, bringing the month back to something beautifully simple: what actually makes you feel safe? A financial development, purchase, income shift, or realization about your self-worth could help you end October with a much more grounded definition of security and love.

Taurus Sun & Rising:

Taurus, October may show you that the people closest to you are revealing just as much about your evolution as your own inner work is. With Venus, your ruling planet, retrograding through Scorpio at the beginning of the month and Mercury retrograding there later on, relationships become one of your biggest mirrors. Rather than simply asking who stays and who goes, you may start noticing subtler dynamics: who brings out your defensiveness, who makes you feel more powerful, who you perform calmness around, and which connections still operate according to an older version of you. The month can deepen certain bonds considerably, but only if there is enough honesty for both people to acknowledge what has changed.

Mid-month, Pluto stations direct in Aquarius in your career and public-image sector, giving more momentum to a professional transformation that has probably been unfolding beneath the surface for months. You may feel more comfortable claiming authority, changing how you present your work, or stepping away from an industry expectation that no longer fits you. There can also be a stronger desire to build influence on your own terms rather than chasing conventional approval. The moves you make now may look bolder from the outside because internally, you have already spent months questioning what kind of success is actually worth having.

Once Scorpio Season begins on October 23rd, relationships become even harder to treat casually, and you may crave more depth, loyalty, and emotional presence from the people around you. Then the Taurus Full Moon on October 26th lands in your sign, bringing the focus decisively back to you. Something about your identity, body, appearance, personal direction, or emotional needs may reach a culmination, and after a month spent examining relationships, this Full Moon can feel like coming home to yourself. You may end October much clearer about who you are becoming, and much less willing to shape that person around someone else’s expectations.

Gemini Sun & Rising:

Gemini, October may make you realize that some of your most “productive” habits have actually been sophisticated forms of avoidance. Venus retrogrades through Scorpio at the beginning of the month, and your ruler Mercury retrogrades there later on, keeping your work, wellness, and daily-life sector under review almost all month. You may question how much of your routine genuinely supports you versus how much simply keeps you busy enough not to feel what is underneath. Old work patterns, burnout cycles, body-image narratives, or even a job dynamic you thought you had outgrown could resurface, giving you a chance to rebuild your day-to-day life around what actually makes you feel well.

Mid-month, Pluto stations direct in Aquarius in your expansion realm, and this can feel like your worldview starts moving again after months of deep internal questioning. You may feel more willing to publish, teach, travel, study, speak on a bigger platform, or commit to a perspective that feels more authentically yours. There can be a contrarian edge to this shift too; you may care less about whether your beliefs are widely approved of and more about whether they are intellectually honest.

Once Scorpio Season begins on October 23rd, your attention turns even more strongly toward your body, workload, and the systems that keep your life functioning. Then the Taurus Full Moon on October 26th illuminates your solitude and subconscious zone, which may be the real exhale of the month. You could suddenly understand why you’ve been so tired, why a certain fear keeps repeating, or why you need more privacy than usual. Give yourself room to disappear from the noise for a minute; some answers arrive only after your nervous system stops performing for everyone else.

Cancer Sun & Rising:

Cancer, October may reconnect you with parts of yourself you’ve been too busy protecting to fully enjoy. Venus retrogrades through Scorpio early in the month, and Mercury retrogrades there later on, keeping your romance, creativity, pleasure, and inner-child realm under review. You may find yourself revisiting an old creative dream, questioning what kind of attention actually feels nourishing, or noticing where fear of disappointment has made you overly cautious in love. Because this is a fellow Water sign, the emotional material can run deep, but that can be useful; the month may help you understand why certain desires still matter and which ones have simply been waiting for you to feel safe enough to claim them again.

Mid-month, Pluto stations direct in Aquarius in your intimacy, shared-resources, and transformation sector, helping you regain momentum around something that has required real emotional excavation. A financial arrangement, debt, trust issue, power dynamic, or deeply private fear may start to feel more manageable because you are seeing it more clearly now. You may also become more comfortable asking for support instead of assuming you have to carry everything alone. The inner work of the retrograde period can translate into stronger boundaries and more strategic decisions.

Once Scorpio Season begins on October 23rd, your creative and romantic world becomes even more vivid, and you may feel ready to take pleasure more seriously. Then the Taurus Full Moon on October 26th lights up your friendship, community, and future-goals zone, grounding all that emotion in something collective and tangible. A friendship may deepen, a social goal may culminate, or you may realize which people actually make your future feel more possible. By month’s end, joy may feel less like an escape and more like part of the life you are deliberately building.

Leo Sun & Rising:

Leo, October may feel like a month of realizing that confidence gets a lot more powerful when your private life can actually support it. Venus retrogrades through Scorpio at the beginning of the month, and Mercury retrogrades there later on, keeping your home, family, roots, and emotional foundation under review. You may revisit an old family dynamic, rethink what “home” means to you, or become aware of how much certain private tensions have been draining energy from the version of you everyone else sees. This month can bring nostalgia, tenderness, and even a little moodiness, but the point is to understand what kind of emotional environment actually allows you to thrive.

Mid-month, Pluto stations direct in Aquarius in your partnership sector, and that can bring more clarity around relationships that have been changing you from the inside out. You may feel more willing to address power dynamics directly, redefine the terms of a commitment, or admit that a connection has been asking you to evolve in ways you can no longer avoid. There can also be a stronger attraction to people who challenge your assumptions rather than simply validate them. The deeper question is whether your relationships are helping you become more fully yourself.

Once Scorpio Season begins on October 23rd, your attention turns even more inward toward home, family, and emotional security, which creates an interesting contrast with Mars energizing your sign all month. Then the Taurus Full Moon on October 26th illuminates your career and public-image realm, potentially bringing recognition, a professional culmination, or a clearer sense of where you want to be seen. The tension between private needs and public ambition may be impossible to ignore by month’s end, but it can also help you build a version of success that does not require sacrificing your inner peace.

Virgo Sun & Rising:

Virgo, October may have you questioning whether the way you communicate is actually protecting your peace or just creating more pressure. Venus retrogrades through Scorpio at the beginning of the month, and your ruler Mercury retrogrades there later on, keeping your communication, learning, and immediate environment under review. Old conversations may resurface, misunderstandings may reveal deeper emotional layers, and you could become much more aware of how often you edit yourself before speaking. This month can help you distinguish between thoughtful communication and over-managing everyone’s reactions, especially if you’ve been carrying words you never quite said.

Mid-month, Pluto stations direct in Aquarius in your work, wellness, and routine sector, helping you regain momentum around habits or systems that have been undergoing a deeper transformation. You may feel more ready to change how you structure your day, address an unhealthy work pattern, or take your energy levels more seriously. There can also be a shift in how much control you try to exert over productivity; what matters now is building routines that are powerful because they’re sustainable, not because they keep you in a constant state of vigilance.

Once Scorpio Season begins on October 23rd, your mental world gets even more intense, and you may crave fewer but more meaningful conversations. Then the Taurus Full Moon on October 26th illuminates your expansion realm, bringing a bigger-picture realization around travel, education, publishing, spirituality, or where your life is headed next. After a month of examining the details so closely, this Full Moon can help you zoom out and see which path actually gives all that effort a sense of purpose.

Libra Sun & Rising:

Libra, October may ask you to get much more specific about what you value once the birthday-season glow wears off. Venus, your ruling planet, retrogrades through Scorpio at the beginning of the month, and Mercury retrogrades there later on, keeping your money, self-worth, and security realm under review. You may rethink spending habits, pricing, what you consider “worth it,” or the ways you sometimes tie being loved to being generous. There can also be a creative reassessment here: what are you investing time and money into because it genuinely matters to you, and what are you maintaining out of habit, image, or guilt? The month can help you build a more honest relationship with your definition of “enough.”

Mid-month, Pluto stations direct in Aquarius in your romance, creativity, fate, and inner-child sector, and this can feel like something starts moving again around joy. A love story, creative pursuit, passion project, or even your relationship with visibility may feel less psychologically complicated than it did during the retrograde. You may be more willing to take yourself seriously as an artist, lover, or creator, and less willing to make yourself smaller just to keep the peace. There is a stronger sense that pleasure can be transformative too.

Once Scorpio Season begins on October 23rd, questions around money, value, and emotional security become even harder to ignore, but the Taurus Full Moon on October 26th shifts the focus toward intimacy, trust, and shared resources. A financial agreement, relationship dynamic, debt, or deeper emotional exchange may reach a turning point. The month may end by showing you that security is not only about what you possess on your own; it’s also about knowing which people and arrangements are stable enough for you to safely merge with.

Scorpio Sun & Rising:

Scorpio, October may feel less like a reinvention and more like a reckoning with the version of yourself you’ve been outgrowing. Venus retrogrades through your sign at the beginning of the month, and Mercury retrogrades there later on, keeping your identity, appearance, desires, relationships, and personal choices under review. You may find yourself revisiting old versions of yourself, old attractions, or old ways of moving through the world and realizing some of them no longer fit. Because both retrogrades are happening in your sign, this month can feel especially personal, but also deeply clarifying. You’re being asked to notice what you still want, what you only wanted because it once made you feel powerful, and what parts of yourself are ready to be reclaimed.

Mid-month, Pluto stations direct in Aquarius in your home, family, and emotional foundation sector, which can help something beneath the surface begin to shift more decisively. A family dynamic, living situation, ancestral pattern, or private emotional reality may start feeling less stuck, even if the external change is subtle at first. You may feel more ready to make your home reflect who you are becoming, set firmer boundaries with relatives, or stop carrying emotional roles that were never really yours to begin with.

Once Scorpio Season begins on October 23rd, your birthday season is activated and your energy starts returning to center stage, but Mercury starting its retrograde the very next day means this is still more of a reflective rebirth than a clean launch. Then the Taurus Full Moon on October 26th illuminates your partnership sector, bringing a
relationship, collaboration, or one-on-one dynamic into sharper focus. After a month of questioning yourself so deeply, this Full Moon may show you which relationships can actually meet the person you’re becoming rather than the person they first met.

Sagittarius Sun & Rising:

Sag, October may prove that sometimes the clearest answers arrive when you stop trying to outrun the question. Venus retrogrades through Scorpio at the beginning of the month, and Mercury retrogrades there later on, creating a month-long review in your solitude, subconscious, healing, and closure zone. Dreams may become more vivid, old feelings could return without warning, and you may crave considerably more privacy than usual. A past relationship or creative desire could occupy your thoughts again, but its return does not automatically mean it belongs in your future. Pay attention to what your subconscious is revealing about the desires, fears, and emotional loose ends you normally stay busy enough to avoid.

Mid-month, Pluto stations direct in Aquarius in your communication, learning, and local-community realm, and your voice may feel noticeably more powerful. After months of privately reconsidering how you think, speak, write, or share your ideas, you may feel ready to communicate something with greater conviction, even if your perspective disrupts the room a little. This can also deepen your relationship with writing, teaching, media, or storytelling. You’ve been transforming the way you think; now people may begin noticing the difference in how you express it.

Once Scorpio Season begins on October 23rd, your need for rest and reflection becomes even harder to ignore, so resist treating this quieter chapter like a productivity problem. Then the Taurus Full Moon on October 26th illuminates your work, health, and daily-routine sector, bringing something very practical into focus. You may realize that a schedule, workload, wellness habit, or responsibility needs to change because your body simply cannot keep negotiating with it. After such an internal month, this Full Moon helps you translate what your soul has been saying into something your everyday life can actually sustain.

Capricorn Sun & Rising:

Capricorn, October may show you that your future’s changing because your standards for who gets to come with you are changing too. Venus retrogrades through Scorpio at the beginning of the month, and Mercury retrogrades there later on, keeping your friendship, community, collaboration, and long-term goals under review. title: A Week In Dallas, TX On A $53,000 Salary
text:
A Week In Dallas, TX On A $53,000 Salary

Welcome to Money Diaries where we are tackling the ever-present taboo that is money. We’re asking real people how they spend their hard-earned money during a seven-day period — and we’re tracking every last dollar.

This week: An associate working in apparel who makes $53,000 per year and spends some of it on some kiwis (an out-of-the-ordinary purchase for me!).

If you’d like to submit your own Money Diary, you can do so via our online form. We pay $150 for each published diary. Apologies but we’re not able to reply to every email. We are legally unable to publish any diaries that have been written with the use of AI.

Interested in taking our latest Money Diaries survey? We’d love to hear your thoughts here.

Occupation: Associate
Industry: Apparel
Age: 26
Location: Dallas, TX
Salary: $53,000
Joint Income/Financial Setup: n/a
Assets:
Savings: $793.62 (I recently went to Hawaii for vacation, and that wiped out a bit of my savings despite traveling on the cheap, staying in hostels etc).
Debt: $33,386.42 (My student loans plus credit card debt)
Paycheck Amount (2x month): $1,803
Pronouns: She/her

Monthly Expenses

Housing Costs: $1,265 (I live alone in a one-bedroom apartment).
Loan Payments: $1,803
Utilities (electricity & water): ~$100
Nuuly subscription: $106.09 (I forgot to cancel it last month, oops!)
Gym membership: $95
Web portfolio: $8

Was there an expectation for you to attend higher education? Did you participate in any form of higher education? If yes, how did you pay for it?
Yes, I got my bachelor’s degree from the same school my family’s three generations of women went to. When I received a partial academic scholarship, that was that! I’m currently paying it back with state and federal loans.

Growing up, what kind of conversations did you have about money? Did your parent(s) educate you about finances?
Other than vague, dad statements of “you need to save!” etc., we didn’t really talk about actionable steps/financial literacy in our house. To me, money has always felt very stressful and confusing to navigate. I want to be “good” at saving, etc., but it can feel overwhelming. I loved writing this Money Diary as an exercise to track my spending, so hopefully it’s the start of better money habits.

What was your first job and why did you get it?
I had a front-desk job at a country club during college (my cousin who had also worked there referred me). I answered phones, refilled water/coffee, managed schedules and was generally helpful. It was excellent money and a very low-stress job! My parents helped pay for my rent in college, but I was expected to pay for gas, groceries, and other needs.

Did you worry about money growing up?
I remember a couple of times growing up when I realized we were sort of “cutting back” as a family. But, fortunately, no dire circumstances. In terms of handling my own money, I remember wanting to give away any I had accumulated — this being maybe $20 at most, made from neighborhood donut stands or “cleaning” my grandmother’s room. I think my kid brain thought I’d be no good at handling it and/or sensing it would be stressful to manage. I just wanted someone else to have it and be done.

Do you worry about money now?
Yes, especially since I was recently passed over for a raise and I make the lowest salary within the company. I struggle to find a balance between accruing savings while paying off my student loans/credit card debt. I worry constantly about being the sort of person who is good at saving, good at spending, good at maximizing credit card points — I definitely don’t understand credit card points!

At what age did you become financially responsible for yourself and do you have a financial safety net?
I became fully financially responsible for myself post-grad at 22 years old, when I got my first full-time job. I would say my parents are my “financial safety net,” although since my mom just lost her job — and they are helping pay back some of my brother’s student loans, which accumulated — that would be an absolute last resort.

Do you or have you ever received passive or inherited income? If yes, please explain.
I received $5,000 from my aunt in her will and used the majority of it to pay off one of my credit cards.

DashDividers_1_500x100

Day One: Monday

7 a.m. — I roll out of bed, somewhere between my third and fourth alarm, and become a presentable human. Dress. Brush teeth. Curl bangs. Make coffee smoothie for breakfast. Assemble work bag. Mentally prepare for battle.

11:15 a.m. — I need a pick-me-up, stat! My desk mate and I walk a block over to the local 7/11 gas station. It’s run by a very down-to-earth family who remember their regular customers. They handle a lot of craziness (it’s open 24/7). I gather the makings of a gas station charcuterie board for lunch: pickles, meat stick, chocolate peanut butter energy bar and an energy drink! I finally signed up for the 7/11 app and plan to cash in on my points later this week! $11.93

5:20 p.m. — Post-work I head to grocery store and think about my co-worker who got fired — it’s very upsetting! I park, head in and realize I have had a stain on the back of my shirt all day! Ack! I hate that. Grocery haul includes kiwi, salami, turkey deli meat, kombucha, chickpea pasta, kale, beets, sweet potato, chicken breasts, chocolate, granola, orange juice, almonds, tortilla chips and salsa. As much as I love Sprouts, my neighborhood grocery store is definitely cheaper and the member deals make a big difference in total. $97.99

6:20 p.m. — I’m home now, so I feast upon salami, cheese, almonds, and peach kombucha while reading my book on my apartment’s outdoor patio.

7:00 p.m. — I start to get ready for the gym and decide to stop for a brief bang cutting interlude (slightly too short, but what can you do!) and then head out.

8:45 p.m. — Once home, I tidy up a little bit, “stain clinic” my soiled shirt and start a load of washing, while avoiding eye contact with the dirty dishes in the sink.

10:00 p.m. — Shower! Cozy and in bed, I pick up where I left off in my book: Maybe You Should Talk to Someone by Lori Gottlieb. I’m considering art therapy as a potential career path and I love hearing the therapists POV on a therapy session.

Daily Total: $109.92

DashDividers_1_500x100

Day Two: Tuesday

7 a.m. — I wake up and make Laird Superfood coffee; it’s so good! I heat up frozen sausage, and chuck a yogurt in my bag. I quickly assemble a salad with cranberries, blue cheese, turkey, and greens for lunch (while genius-ly repurposing the kiwi box as my Tupperware container). I’m heading to the warehouse for work. It’s truly so dirty, but the people there are nice. I mentally black out for the rest of the day because I hate the warehouse.

5 p.m. — Eventually, it’s over and I head to my gym for my 6 p.m. workout class — the cost is included in my monthly membership. I get there early and work on my computer using the gym’s wifi.

8 p.m. — Workout class done *fist bump*. I drive to my parents’ house to work from home the next day. They live about 45-minute drive away. I get home in time to scavenge the leftovers of my parents’ dinner: chicken, rice, and beans from a local TexMex place I love. We veg in front of the TV and catch up.

Daily Total: $0

DashDividers_1_500x100

Day Three: Wednesday

7:55 a.m. — Since it’s a WFH day I wake up leisurely at 7:55 a.m. My mom goes out to get us Starbucks — egg bites and lattes. Mom pays!

12:00 p.m. — For lunch, we make chicken soup with salad and sip on tea. I coo over my cat, who is recovering from a bite wound. She’s 80% back to normal, but still limps around the house. I baby her and let her drink water from the tap when my mom isn’t looking.

5:00 p.m. — I head back to Dallas to meet a friend for a ropes climbing session at 6 p.m. We talk, catch up, and I climb my first 11c grade route! By the end of our workout, I’m dying for a Gatorade Lime Cucumber but it’s all sold out. Drat! I settle for boring lemon/lime flavor and charge it to my membership, like a fancy kid! $4

9:00 p.m. — I get home, shower, make chickpea pasta with olive oil and black olives. Nothing fancy but it works! Then conk the heck out.

Daily Total: $4

DashDividers_1_500x100

Day Four: Thursday

7:00 a.m. — Surprise, surprise, I’m headed to the dirty old warehouse! My boss will not be there today, so things will be a bit more lax. I munch on chocolate chip granola and sip kombucha from my grocery haul, hoping it will give me enough caffeine to last the day.

12:30 p.m. — I didn’t bring lunch, so I drive over to a local cafe for my “usual”: fresh salad with cranberries, cheese, and chicken with a pink berry dressing, plus I leave a tip. I bring the food back to the warehouse and enjoy the breeze from the porch. $16.24

5:00 p.m. — I’m supposed to meet my cousin for tennis, but it’s just rained and the courts are likely wet. We reschedule and I head to the SMU Meadows Museum instead. It’s free entry on Thursday evenings. There’s a special Raimundo de Madrazo exhibit on display, which the art history student (my assumption) at the front desk recommends. The Belle Époque portraits are vibrant and really realistic! I feel so cultured.

7:00 p.m. — I get home and try to cook veggies in the oven but accidentally set off the fire alarm! I jump out of the shower and fan the fire alarm with a towel on and shampoo in my hair. I end up making a salad with turkey instead, blah! Then Venmo my friend who I have been meaning to pay back since our Hawaii vacation. $150

Daily Total: $166.24

DashDividers_1_500x100

Day Five: Friday

7:00 a.m. — Friday! I make a smoothie with banana, peanut butter, and coffee and saddle up for the day. On the way to the warehouse, I stop at a gas station to buy spring water and a macadamia nut Clif bar (arguably the best flavor!) My boss ends up bringing me an energy drink, and even though I’ve been trying to quit drinking these, my smoothie turned out to be gross, so I sip on it throughout the day. I become extra caffeinated. Cost: FREEEEEEEEEEEEE! $4.88

12:30 p.m. — My boss wants to eat off campus so we head to an outside food hall with a bunch of different stalls. I get a spicy pork bulgogi bowl and a yuzu lemonade (plus tip) from the Korean place. So, so yummy! We lunch al fresco and my boss talks about work. Fun! $28.12

4:30 p.m. — It’s a Friday miracle because we got out of work early! On the way home, I stop at Walgreens and purchase hand soap, bathroom tissue, and Lanolips lip balm. I thought it was on sale. It was not. I purchase anyway for my split lip. $56.73

6:00 p.m. — I meet my friend to climb and he’s gotten a haircut which totally throws me off. We climb and I pretend not to stare at his haircut the whole time.

8:00 p.m. — I driver over to my cousin’s apartment to help her make cookies for a luncheon tomorrow. We catch up, nibble on cookie dough, and make a frozen pizza for dinner then I head home!

Daily Total: $89.73

DashDividers_1_500x100

Day Six: Saturday

10:30 a.m. — I wake up at exactly the time the luncheon starts — oops! It’s informal but I hate that I’m immediately late. I text my cousin I’m on my way, and brush my teeth while simultaneously making coffee and dressing myself! The dress — courtesy of this month’s accidental Nuuly subscription — is a lovely, white linen thing with pink ric-rac trim and a back cut-out. I set out ready to seize the day!

11:00 a.m. — I arrive and munch on sugar cookies, sip coffee, and meet new people. I get third place in Bunco and leave with a set of party cups illustrated by an artist my mom adores (I’m mentally noting to gift these to her).

3:00 p.m. — By the time I make it home, I’m very hungry. I snack on buckwheat English muffins slathered in butter and peanut butter, a honey crisp apple, and finish my morning coffee. While passing the mirror, I realize you can sort of see my underwear through the dress! I bombard my cousin with texts, asking if she could see my underwear. She says no but I suspect she’s lying. The underwear was patterned with the Victoria’s Secret pink dog across my bum…

4:00 p.m. — It’s about this time of day that I find myself at IKEA (my happy place) and buy a summery green gingham bed cover, a sink brush, and cutting boards! Getting functional home stuff that excites me is one of the ways I motivate myself to clean/take better care of my space. I had been seriously eyeing some of their standalone kitchen islands (I have next to no counterspace in my apartment) but leave without making any big purchases. $57.34

5:00 p.m. — I stop at a nearby Whole Foods and buy snacks for when I’ll be working on my computer later at Half Price Books. I get a fancy lemonade and cocoa energy bites. $15.46

7:00 p.m. — After some productive writing at HPB and a little eavesdropping (my seat mates were having a very intense philosophical discussion) I head home. I want to make a casserole, so I boil chicken breasts for, I want to say, eternity? I set the heat too low! The casserole also calls for rice simmered in chicken stock, frozen peas, and cheese. It takes way longer than expected, but I enjoy the warm casserole for dinner, yummy! I then put the rest in the fridge.

10:00 p.m. — I finish my book and then hit the hay.

Daily Total: $72.80

DashDividers_1_500x100

Day Seven: Sunday

7:15 a.m. — I wake up and get dressed for church. I make my coffee and go to add a finishing splash of creamer. Only it’s too late when I realize I’ve poured chunky expired creamer in instead of fresh creamer. Nooo! (You might be asking why I haven’t thrown out the old one yet, but I just keep forgetting). I’m dismayed and put the chunky creamer back into the fridge. I sing along to “Lake Street Dive” in the car while I drive over.

10:30 a.m. — Church is over and I still have a hankering for coffee. I decide to try a Yemeni coffee place I read about in Eater Magazine. It’s designed beautifully with lots of white marble and I beeline to the colorful pastry case. I choose Oreo covered dates to go with my latte. When my coffee is ready, I see they’ve made a latte art camel! I’m very content as I sip my coffee and work on my computer. $11.51

12:30 p.m. — On the way home, I stop at a gas station where they have longhorns and donkeys corralled outside. I get gas and say hi to the animals. They hide from me instead. I step in a mud puddle in my flip flops, damn.

1:00 p.m. — Once home, I eat the second half of my pork bowl from Friday for lunch. I read my new book Garlic and Sapphires: The Secret Life of a Critic in Disguise by Ruth Reichl (food critic queen!) and chill out. $68.14

5:30 p.m. — In the evening, I head to a local track and try sprints but gosh it’s been too long! I swear there’s someone there who must be training for the Olympics! Even though I make only a little progress I’m satisfied. I head home, shower, and make an omelet (olive oil, eggs, no frills) for dinner like I’m living in a Danielle Steel novel.

Daily Total: $79.65

DashDividers_1_500x100

The Breakdown

Conclusion:
I definitely mooched on other people for food this week, ha! I think my grocery haul set me up for success because typically I eat out a bit more for lunch, especially when working at the warehouse. I’d like to continue to be more mindful with my grocery purchases because that makes a big difference in spending — eating out is a nice treat but doing that almost every day certainly adds up. Another conclusion I came to is I’d like to become more financially literate. I’d like to find books or a course that could help me maximize my earnings/savings/cc points, etc.

Money Diaries are meant to reflect an individual’s experience and do not necessarily reflect Refinery29’s point of view. Refinery29 in no way encourages illegal activity or harmful behavior.

title: The Old Navy x Altuzarra Collab Is Here: Zac Posen & Joseph Altuzarra Break Down The Fall Capsule
text:
The Old Navy x Altuzarra Collab Is Here: Zac Posen & Joseph Altuzarra Break Down The Fall Capsule

With fall officially here, there’s a chill in the air, leaves are falling, our couches are calling us to cozy up with a good book, and (in my opinion) it’s the best fashion season. To dress us for all the fall activities (and help us channel our best Cathy), Old Navy has teamed up with Altuzarra on an enchanting collaboration.

“Drawing inspiration from the Regency and early Victorian literary eras, the collection reflects the romance and mystery of classic Romantic and Gothic fiction,” according to a press release. Inspired by Wuthering Heights, these designs are meant to be worn passionately (and to frolic through wide fields in). It’s also the first time one of Old Navy’s collaborations features styles across women’s, girls’, and toddlers’ for matching family moments.

Ahead, I speak with Old Navy’s Chief Creative Officer Zac Posen and Altuzarra’s Creative Director Joseph Altuzarra to learn about how this collaboration came about and their favorite styles to build fall outfits with. Then shop the limited-time collection, which ranges from $24 to $140, on Old Navy’s website on September 30.
